Abstract.

We study the local and global wellposedness of a full system of Magneto-Hydro-Dynamic equations. The system is a coupling of the forced (Lorentz force) incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with the Maxwell equations through Ohm’s law for the current. We show the local existence of mild solutions for arbitrarily large data in a space similar to the scale invariant spaces classically used for Navier-Stokes. These solutions are global if the initial data are small enough. Our results not only simplify and unify the proofs for the space dimensions two and three but also refine those in [10]. The main simplification comes from an a priori Lt2​(Lx∞)L^{2}_{t}(L^{\infty}_{x}) estimate for solutions of the forced Navier-Stokes equations.

Key words and phrases: 
Navier-Stokes equations, Maxwell equations, MHD, global well-posedness.
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
35Q30, 82C31, 76A05.

1. Introduction

The purpose of this paper is the study of the following full Magneto-Hydro-Dynamics system (MHD):

(1.1) {∂v∂t+v⋅∇v−ν​Δ​v+∇p=j×B∂tE−curl​B=−j∂tB+curl​E=0div​v=div​B=0σ⁡(E+v×B)=j\ \left\{\begin{array}[]{rclll}\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}+v\cdot\nabla v-\nu\Delta v+\nabla p&=&j{{\times}}B\\ \partial_{t}E-{\rm curl}\,B&=&-j\\ \partial_{t}B+{\rm curl}\,E&=&0&\\ {\rm div}v={\rm div}B&=&0\\ \sigma(E+v{{\times}}B)&=&j\end{array}\right.

subject to the initial data

v|t=0=v0,B|t=0=B0,E|t=0=E0.v_{|t=0}=v^{0},\quad B_{|t=0}=B^{0},\quad E_{|t=0}=E^{0}.

Here, v,E,B:ℝt+×ℝxd⟶ℝ3v,E,B:\mathbb{R}^{+}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}_{x}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3} are vector fields defined on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (d=2d=2 or 33). The vector field v=(v1,…,vd)v=(v_{1},...,v_{d}) is the velocity of the fluid, ν\nu its viscosity and the scalar function pp stands for the pressure. The vector fields EE and BB are the electric and magnetic fields, respectively, and jj is the electric current given by Ohm’s law (the fifth equation of the system, where σ\sigma is the electric resistivity). The force term j×Bj\times B in the Navier-Stokes equations comes from the Lorentz force under a quasi-neutrality assumption of the net charge carried by the fluid. Note that the pressure pp can be recovered from vv and j×Bj\times B via an explicit Caldéron-Zygmund operator (see [5] for instance). The second equation in (1.1) is the Ampère-Maxwell equation for an electric field EE. The third equation is nothing but Faraday’s law. For a detailed introduction to MHD, we refer to Davidson [8] and Biskamp [2].

Note that in the 2D case, the functions vv, EE, BB, and jj are defined on the whole space ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with values in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. In this case, the operator ∇\nabla is given by

∇=(∂x1,∂x2,0)T.\nabla=(\partial_{x_{1}},\partial_{x_{2}},0)^{T}.

Thus

div⁡v:=∂x1v1+∂x2v2,∇p:=(∂x1p,∂x2p,0)T,\operatorname{div}v:=\partial_{x_{1}}v_{1}+\partial_{x_{2}}v_{2},\quad\nabla p:=(\partial_{x_{1}}p,\partial_{x_{2}}p,0)^{T},

and

curlF:=(∂x2F3,−∂x1F3,∂x1F2−∂x2F1)T.\hbox{curl}\,F:=(\partial_{x_{2}}F_{3},-\partial_{x_{1}}F_{3},\partial_{x_{1}}F_{2}-\partial_{x_{2}}F_{1})^{T}.

In the following, we take σ=ν=1\sigma=\nu=1 to alleviate the notations.

Multiply the Navier-Stokes equations in (1.1) by vv, the Ampère-Maxwell equations by (B,E)T(B,E)^{T} and integrate (using the divergence free condition on the velocity); this gives the formal energy identity

12​dd​t​[‖v‖L22+‖B‖L22+‖E‖L22]+‖j‖L22+‖∇v‖L22=0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\big[\|v\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|B\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|E\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\big]+\|j\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=0.

This identity shows that the energy is dissipated by the viscosity and the electric resistivity. It also suggests that one should be able to construct a global finite energy weak solution (à la Leray) for data lying in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). However, this intuitive expectation remains an interesting open problem for (1.1) in both dimensions d=2,3d=2,3. Indeed, given a standard approximating scheme, it is hard to obtain compactness of the solutions, especially for the magnetic field due to the hyperbolicity of Maxwell’s equations. In dimension 2, the equation is energy critical, but running a fixed point argument for data (v0,E0,B0)(v^{0},E^{0},B^{0}) only in L2​(ℝd)3L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{3} seems very difficult due to the term E×BE\times B.

Imposing more regularity on the initial electro-magnetic field, existence results are known. Recently, for initial data (v0,E0,B0)∈L2​(ℝ2)×(Hs​(ℝ2))2(v^{0},E^{0},B^{0})\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\times\big(H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\big)^{2} with s>0s>0, Masmoudi in [14] proved the existence and uniqueness of global strong solutions to (1.1). His proof relies on the use of the energy inequality combined with a logarithmic inequality that enabled him to upper estimate the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the velocity field by the energy norm and higher Sobolev norms. It is also interesting to note that the proof in [14] does not use the divergence free condition of the magnetic field, nor the decay property of the linear part coming from Maxwell’s equations, namely

(1.2) {∂E∂t−curl​B+E=f,∂B∂t+curl​E=0,∇⋅B=0.\ \left\{\begin{array}[]{rclll}\frac{\partial E}{\partial t}-\hbox{curl}\,\,B+E&=&f,\\ \\ \frac{\partial B}{\partial t}+\hbox{curl}\,\,E&=&0,\\ \\ \nabla\cdot B&=&0.\end{array}\right.

Another line of research was pursued by Ibrahim and Keraani [10] who considered data (v0,E0,B0)∈B˙2,11/2​(ℝ3)×(H˙1/2​(ℝ3))2(v_{0},E_{0},B_{0})\in\dot{B}^{1/2}_{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\times\big(\dot{H}^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\big)^{2} in dimension d=3d=3, and (v0,E0,B0)∈B˙2,10​(ℝ2)×(Ll​o​g2​(ℝ2))2(v_{0},E_{0},B_{0})\in\dot{B}^{0}_{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\times\big(L^{2}_{log}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\big)^{2} in dimension d=2d=2 (see below for the definiton of these functional spaces). These authors built up strong solutions by using parabolic regularization arguments giving control of the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the velocity field of the solution. More recently, Ibrahim and Yoneda constructed local in time solution for non-decaying initial data on the torus. See [11] for more details.

In this paper, we follow up on the work of Ibrahim and Keraani by running a fixed point argument to obtain mild solutions, but taking the initial velocity field in the natural Navier-Stokes space Hd2−1H^{\frac{d}{2}-1}. Our main theorem extends the earlier results that were mentioned in many respects: the regularity of the initial velocity and electromagnetic fields is lowered, and we unify the proofs in the cases of space dimension 2 and 3. One of the key ingredients will be to use an L2​L∞L^{2}L^{\infty} estimate on the velocity field, which simplifies greatly the fixed point argument; in particular, the weak decay for the electromagnetic field is not needed any more in dimension 3.

Before stating our main result, we need a few definitions.

Definition 1.1.

First, let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the Leray projection on divergence-free vector fields.

A function Γ:=(v,E,B)\Gamma:=(v,E,B) with div⁡(v)=div⁡(B)=0{\rm div}(v)={\rm div}(B)=0 is said to be a mild solution on a time interval [0,T][0,T] of the full MHD problem (1.1) if Γ∈𝒞⁡([0,T],H˙d2−1)\Gamma\in{\mathcal{C}}([0,T],\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1}) and satisfies the integral equation

Γ⁡(t)=et​𝒜​Γ​(0)+∫0te(t−t′)​𝒜​𝒩​(Γ⁡(t′))​d​t′,\Gamma(t)=e^{t{\mathcal{A}}}\Gamma(0)+\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-t^{\prime}){\mathcal{A}}}{\mathcal{N}}(\Gamma(t^{\prime}))\;dt^{\prime},

with

𝒜=(Δ000−Icurl0−curl0){\mathcal{A}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\Delta&0&0\\ 0&-I&{\rm curl}\\ 0&-{\rm curl}&0\end{array}\right)

and 𝒩(Γ)=(𝒫(−∇(v⊗v)+E×B+(v×B)×B),−v×B,0)T{\mathcal{N}}(\Gamma)=\big({\mathcal{P}}(-\nabla(v\otimes v)+E\times B+(v\times B)\times B),-v\times B,0\big)^{T}.

The functional analytic framework we will use is the following.

Definition 1.2.

Let Δq\Delta_{q} denote the dyadic frequency localization operator defined in section 2. For s,t∈ℝs,t\in\mathbb{R} and α≥0\alpha\geq 0 define the space H˙αs,t{\dot{H}}^{s,t}_{\alpha} by its norm

‖ϕ‖H˙αs,t2:=∑q≤022​q​s​‖Δq​ϕ‖L22+∑q>0qα​22​q​t​‖Δq​ϕ‖L22.\|\phi\|_{\dot{H}^{s,t}_{\alpha}}^{2}:=\sum_{q\leq 0}2^{2qs}\|\Delta_{q}\phi\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\sum_{q>0}q^{\alpha}2^{2qt}\|\Delta_{q}\phi\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

We will also use the short-hands

H˙s=H˙0s,s,H˙logs:=H˙1s,sandH˙s,t:=H˙0s,t.\dot{H}^{s}=\dot{H}^{s,s}_{0}\quad,\quad\dot{H}^{s}_{\rm log}:=\dot{H}^{s,s}_{1}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\dot{H}^{s,t}:=\dot{H}^{s,t}_{0}.

Finally, define L~Tr​H˙αs,t\tilde{L}^{r}_{T}{{\dot{H}}^{s,t}_{\alpha}} by its norm

‖ϕ‖L~Tr​H˙αs,t2:=∑q≤022​q​s​‖Δq​ϕ‖LTr​L22+∑q>0qα​22​q​t​‖Δq​ϕ‖LTr​L22,\|\phi\|_{\tilde{L}^{r}_{T}{{\dot{H}}^{s,t}_{\alpha}}}^{2}:=\sum_{q\leq 0}2^{2qs}\|\Delta_{q}\phi\|_{L^{r}_{T}L^{2}}^{2}+\sum_{q>0}q^{\alpha}2^{2qt}\|\Delta_{q}\phi\|_{L^{r}_{T}L^{2}}^{2},

with obvious generalizations to L~Tr​H˙s\tilde{L}^{r}_{T}{\dot{H}}^{s} etc…

The space H˙logs\dot{H}^{s}_{\rm log} is articulated on the standard homogeneous Sobolev space H˙s\dot{H}^{s} with an extra logarithmic weight for the high frequency part. The space H˙s,t\dot{H}^{s,t} is nothing but the usual Sobolev space H˙t\dot{H}^{t} for high frequencies while it behaves like H˙s\dot{H}^{s} for low frequencies. If s>ts>t, it is not difficult to see that H˙s,t=H˙s+H˙t\dot{H}^{s,t}=\dot{H}^{s}+\dot{H}^{t}. The L~\tilde{L} spaces were first used by Chemin and Lerner [7].

Our main result can be stated as follows.

Theorem 1.3.
  • •

    In dimension two and for any

    Γ0:=(v0,E0,B0)∈L2​(ℝ2)×Llog2​(ℝ2)×Llog2​(ℝ2),\Gamma^{0}:=(v^{0},E^{0},B^{0})\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\times L^{2}_{\rm log}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\times L^{2}_{\rm log}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),

    there exists T>0T>0 and a unique mild solution Γ=(v,E,B)\Gamma=(v,E,B) of (1.1) with initial data Γ0\Gamma^{0} and

    v∈L~∞​(0,T,L2)∩L2​(0,T,H˙1∩L∞)E∈L~∞​(0,T,Llog2)∩L2​(0,T,Llog2)B∈L~∞​(0,T,Llog2)∩L2​(0,T,H˙1,0).\begin{split}&v\in\tilde{L}^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2})\cap L^{2}(0,T;\dot{H}^{1}\cap L^{\infty})\\ &E\in\tilde{L}^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}_{\rm log})\cap L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}_{\rm log})\\ &B\in{\tilde{L}}^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}_{\rm log})\cap L^{2}(0,T;\dot{H}^{1,0}).\end{split}

    Moreover, the solution is global (i.e. T=∞T=\infty) if the initial data is sufficiently small in L2×Llog2×Llog2L^{2}\times L^{2}_{\rm log}\times L^{2}_{\rm log}.

  • •

    In dimension three and for any

    Γ0:=(v0,E0,B0)∈H˙12​(ℝ3)×H˙12​(ℝ3)×H˙12​(ℝ3)\Gamma^{0}:=(v^{0},E^{0},B^{0})\in\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\times\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\times\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{3})

    there exists T>0T>0 and a unique mild solution Γ=(v,E,B)\Gamma=(v,E,B) of (1.1) with initial data Γ0\Gamma^{0} and

    v∈L~∞​(0,T,H˙12)∩L2​(0,T,H˙32∩L∞)E∈L~∞​(0,T,H˙12)∩L2​(0,T,H˙12)B∈L~∞​(0,T,H˙12)∩L2​(0,T,H˙32,12).\begin{split}&v\in\tilde{L}^{\infty}(0,T;\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}})\cap L^{2}(0,T;\dot{H}^{\frac{3}{2}}\cap L^{\infty})\\ &E\in\tilde{L}^{\infty}(0,T;\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}})\cap L^{2}(0,T;\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}})\\ &B\in{\tilde{L}}^{\infty}(0,T;\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}})\cap L^{2}(0,T;\dot{H}^{\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}}).\end{split}

    Moreover, the solution is global (i.e. T=∞T=\infty) if the initial data is sufficiently small in H˙12×H˙12×H˙12\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\times\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\times\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}.

In dimension two, the extra logarithmic regularity is needed to estimate the term E×BE\times B appearing in the Navier-Stokes equations.

In dimension three, the control of BB in L2​(0,T,H˙32,12)L^{2}(0,T;\dot{H}^{\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}}) is not needed to close the fixed point estimate, but we added it for completeness.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section we define some further tools needed in the proof. In Section 3, we detail the linear (parabolic regularity) and nonlinear (product law) estimates needed in the proof of the main theorem. The main theorem is then proved in Section 4. Finally, the proofs of some technical estimates are given in the appendix.

3. Linear and Nonlinear estimates

We will make an extensive use of Bernstein’s inequalities (see [5] for instance).

Lemma 3.1 (Bernstein’s lemma).

There exists a constant CC such that for any q,k∈ℕ,q,k\in\mathbb{N}, 1≤a≤b1\leq a\leq b and for f∈La​(ℝd)f\in L^{a}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

sup|α|=k‖∂αSq​f‖Lb\displaystyle\sup_{|\alpha|=k}\|\partial^{\alpha}S_{q}f\|_{L^{b}} ≤\displaystyle\leq Ck​ 2q⁡(k+d⁡(1a−1b))​‖Sq​f‖La,\displaystyle C^{k}\,2^{q(k+d(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}))}\|S_{q}f\|_{L^{a}},
C−k​2q​k​‖Δq​f‖La\displaystyle\ C^{-k}2^{qk}\|{\Delta}_{q}f\|_{L^{a}} ≤\displaystyle\leq sup|α|=k‖∂αΔq​f‖La≤Ck​2q​k​‖Δq​f‖La.\displaystyle\sup_{|\alpha|=k}\|\partial^{\alpha}{\Delta}_{q}f\|_{L^{a}}\leq C^{k}2^{qk}\|{\Delta}_{q}f\|_{L^{a}}.

The parabolic regularity result we will need reads

Lemma 3.2 (Parabolic regularization, see for example [1]).

Let uu be a smooth divergence free vector field solving

{∂tu−Δ​u+∇p=fu|t=0=u0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u+\nabla p=f\\ u_{|t=0}=u^{0},\end{array}\right.

on some time interval [0,T][0,T]. Then, for every p≥r≥1p\geq r\geq 1 and s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} and j≥1j\geq 1,

‖u‖C⁡([0,T],B˙q,js)∩L~Tp​B˙q,js+2p≲‖u0‖B˙q,js+‖f‖L~Tr​B˙q,js−2+2r.\|u\|_{C([0,T];\dot{B}^{s}_{q,j})\cap\tilde{L}^{p}_{T}\dot{B}^{s+\frac{2}{p}}_{q,j}}\lesssim\|u^{0}\|_{\dot{B}^{s}_{q,j}}+\|f\|_{\tilde{L}^{r}_{T}\dot{B}^{s-2+\frac{2}{r}}_{q,j}}.

The following result is an LT2​L∞L^{2}_{T}L^{\infty} estimate which was originally proved in [12], [6] in dimension two.

Lemma 3.3 (L2​L∞L^{2}L^{\infty} estimate).

Let d=2,3d=2,3 and uu be a smooth divergence free vector field solving

{∂tu−Δ​u+∇p=f1+f2u|t=0=u0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u+\nabla p=f_{1}+f_{2}\\ u_{|t=0}=u^{0},\end{array}\right.

on some time interval [0,T][0,T]. Assume that f1∈LT1​H˙d2−1f_{1}\in L^{1}_{T}\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1} and f2∈L~T2​B˙2,1d2−2f_{2}\in\tilde{L}^{2}_{T}\dot{B}^{\frac{d}{2}-2}_{2,1}. Then,

(3.1) ‖u‖LT2​L∞≲‖u0‖H˙d2−1+‖f1‖LT1​H˙d2−1+‖f2‖L~T2​B˙2,1d2−2.\|u\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{\infty}}\lesssim\|u_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1}}+\|f_{1}\|_{L^{1}_{T}\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1}}+\|f_{2}\|_{\tilde{L}^{2}_{T}\dot{B}^{\frac{d}{2}-2}_{2,1}}.
Proof.

Thanks to Lemma 3.2, and using the embeddings

L~2​B˙2,1d/2↪L2​B˙2,1d/2↪L2​L∞,\tilde{L}^{2}\dot{B}^{d/2}_{2,1}\hookrightarrow L^{2}\dot{B}^{d/2}_{2,1}\hookrightarrow L^{2}L^{\infty},

we can assume that f2=0f_{2}=0. Duhamel’s formula gives

u⁡(t)=et​Δ​u0+∫0te(t−t′)​Δ​𝒫​f1​(t′)​d​t′,u(t)=e^{t\Delta}u_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-t^{\prime})\Delta}{\mathcal{P}}f_{1}(t^{\prime})\;dt^{\prime},

Ignoring the time variable, estimate (3.9) is a particular case of the product law

with s1,s2∈]−d2,d2[s_{1},s_{2}\in]-\frac{d}{2},\frac{d}{2}[ and s1+s2>0s_{1}+s_{2}>0. Indeed, it corresponds to the admissible choice s1=s2=12s_{1}=s_{2}=\frac{1}{2}. ur|t=0=u0r,Br|t=0=B0r,Er|t=0=E0r.{u_{r}}_{|t=0}=u^{0}_{r},\quad{B_{r}}_{|t=0}=B^{0}_{r},\quad{E_{r}}_{|t=0}=E^{0}_{r}.

Arguing as in [11], we know that (4.10) has a unique regular solution. Now we solve for (us,Es,Bs)(u_{s},E_{s},B_{s}). We have

(4.11) {∂us∂t+us⋅∇us−Δ​us+us⋅∇ur+ur⋅∇us+∇ps=j×B−jr×Br∂tEs−curl​Bs=j−jr∂tBs+curl​Es=0div​us=div​Bs=0\ \left\{\begin{array}[]{rclll}\frac{\partial u_{s}}{\partial t}+u_{s}\cdot\nabla u_{s}-\Delta u_{s}+u_{s}\cdot\nabla u_{r}+u_{r}\cdot\nabla u_{s}+\nabla p_{s}&=&j\times B-j_{r}\times B_{r}\\ \partial_{t}E_{s}-{\rm curl}\,B_{s}&=&j-j_{r}\\ \partial_{t}B_{s}+{\rm curl}\,E_{s}&=&0&\\ {\rm div}u_{s}={\rm div}B_{s}&=&0\end{array}\right.

subject to the initial data

us|t=0=us0,Bs|t=0=Bs0,E|t=0=E0s.{u_{s}}_{|t=0}=u_{s}^{0},\quad{B_{s}}_{|t=0}=B_{s}^{0},\quad{E}_{|t=0}=E^{0}_{s}.

Proceeding similarly as for the small data result, set

Φ⁡(Γ):=∫0te(t−t′)​𝒜​(𝒫[−us⋅∇us−us⋅∇ur−ur⋅∇us+j×B−jr×Br]j−jr)​d​t′\Phi(\Gamma):=\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{A}}\left(\begin{array}[]{l}\mathcal{P}\left[-u_{s}\cdot\nabla u_{s}-u_{s}\cdot\nabla u_{r}-u_{r}\cdot\nabla u_{s}+j\times B-j_{r}\times B_{r}\right]\\ j-j_{r}\end{array}\right)dt^{\prime}

where Γ\Gamma is defined by

(us,Bs,Es)=et​𝒜​(us0,Bs0,Es0)+Γ.(u_{s},B_{s},E_{s})=e^{t\mathcal{A}}(u_{s}^{0},B_{s}^{0},E_{s}^{0})+\Gamma.

Applying the same proof as for the small data existence, we can show that the map Φ\Phi is a contraction if we choose a time of existence TT sufficiently small. The main difference is that new linear terms (in Γ\Gamma) appear in Φ\Phi. These linear terms need to be small (as linear maps) for Φ\Phi to be a contraction; this can be achieved by using the smoothness of BB and by choosing TT small enough.

For instance:

(4.12) ‖∫0te(t−t′)​Δ​𝒫​Es×Br​d​t′‖𝒵Tu≲‖Es×Br‖LT1​H˙d2−1≲‖Es‖LT∞​H˙d2−1​‖Br‖LT1​H2≲‖Es‖𝒵TE​‖Br‖LT1​H2.\begin{split}\left\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-t^{\prime})\Delta}{\mathcal{P}}E_{s}\times B_{r}\,dt^{\prime}\right\|_{\mathcal{Z}^{u}_{T}}&\lesssim\left\|E_{s}\times B_{r}\right\|_{L^{1}_{T}\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1}}\lesssim\left\|E_{s}\right\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1}}\left\|B_{r}\right\|_{L^{1}_{T}H^{2}}\\ &\lesssim\left\|E_{s}\right\|_{\mathcal{Z}^{E}_{T}}\left\|B_{r}\right\|_{L^{1}_{T}H^{2}}.\end{split}

The key point is of course that ‖Br‖LT1​H2\left\|B_{r}\right\|_{L^{1}_{T}H^{2}} can be made arbitrarily small by choosing TT small enough.

5. Appendix: Proof of the decay for BB and Proposition 3.5

Recall the main part of Lemma 3.3. We emphasize on the fact that this property is an extra information about a weak decay that the magnteic field satisfies and it has no impact on the well posedness result.

Lemma 5.1.

Let α≥0\alpha\geq 0 and G∈LT2​H˙αd2−1G\in L^{2}_{T}\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1}_{\alpha}, and (E,B)(E,B) be a solution of

∂tB+curl​E\displaystyle\partial_{t}B+{\rm curl}\;E =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0\

on some time interval [0,T][0,T]. Then, the following estimate hold with constants not depending upon time

(5.1) ‖B‖L2​H˙αd2,d2−1≲‖(E0,B0)‖H˙αd2−1+‖G‖LT2​H˙αd2−1.\|B\|_{L^{2}\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2},\frac{d}{2}-1}_{\alpha}}\lesssim\|(E_{0},B_{0})\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1}_{\alpha}}+\|G\|_{L^{2}_{T}\dot{H}^{\frac{d}{2}-1}_{\alpha}}.
Proof.

Because of the divergence free property of BB, we have

(5.2) ∂t​tB−ΔB+∂tB=curlG,(B,∂tB)|t=0=(B0,B1).\displaystyle\partial_{tt}B-\Delta B+\partial_{t}B=\hbox{curl}\,G,\qquad(B,\partial_{t}B)_{|t=0}=(B^{0},B^{1}).

Φ1(t,ξ)=e−t/2cosh(1/4−|ξ|2t),Φ2(t,ξ)=e−t/2sinh⁡(1/4−|ξ|2​t)1/4−|ξ|2.\Phi_{1}(t,\xi)=e^{-t/2}\cosh({\sqrt{1/4-|\xi|^{2}}}t),\qquad\Phi_{2}(t,\xi)=e^{-t/2}\frac{\sinh({\sqrt{1/4-|\xi|^{2}}}t)}{\sqrt{1/4-|\xi|^{2}}}.

Proof of Proposition 3.5 The proof is based on the paraproduct decomposition. We choose to prove in details only estimates (3.6) and (3.7). The other estimates are easier or classical and left to the reader.

Proof of (3.6) We decompose E​BEB into

E​B=TE​B+TB​E+S2​R​(E,B)+(I−S2)​R​(E,B),EB=T_{E}B+T_{B}E+S_{2}R(E,B)+(I-S_{2})R(E,B),

and will show the following estimates:

(5.6) ‖TE​B+TB​E‖L~T2​B˙2,1−1​(ℝ2)\displaystyle\|T_{E}B+T_{B}E\|_{\tilde{L}^{2}_{T}\dot{B}^{-1}_{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖E‖LT2​L2​(ℝ2)​‖B‖L~T∞​L2​(ℝ2)\displaystyle\|E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|B\|_{{\tilde{L}}^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}
(5.7) ‖S2​R​(E,B)‖LT1​L2\displaystyle\|S_{2}R(E,B)\|_{L^{1}_{T}L^{2}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖E‖LT2​L2​(ℝ2)​‖B‖LT2​H˙1,0​(ℝ2)\displaystyle\|E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|B\|_{L^{2}_{T}\dot{H}^{1,0}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}
(5.8) ‖(I−S2)​R​(E,B)‖L~T2​ℬ˙2,1−1​(ℝ2)≲‖E‖LT2​Llog2​(ℝ2)​‖B‖L~T∞​Llog2\displaystyle\|(I-S_{2})R(E,B)\|_{{\tilde{L}}^{2}_{T}\dot{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}_{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\lesssim\|E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}_{\rm log}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|B\|_{\tilde{L}^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}_{\rm log}}

First, we prove (5.6). Since the term TB​ET_{B}E can be treated in a very similar way, we focus on TE​BT_{E}B. First,

Δq​(TE​B)=∑|q~−q|≤1Δq​(Δq~​B​Sq~​E).\Delta_{q}(T_{E}B)=\sum_{|{\tilde{q}}-q|\leq 1}\Delta_{q}(\Delta_{\tilde{q}}BS_{\tilde{q}}E).

Since Δq\Delta_{q} is uniformly bounded on L2L^{2}, we have

∑q2−q​‖Δq​(TE​B)‖LT2​L2≲∑q2−q​∑|q~−q|≤1‖Δq~​B​Sq~​E‖LT2​L2.\sum_{q}2^{-q}\|\Delta_{q}(T_{E}B)\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\lesssim\sum_{q}2^{-q}\sum_{|{\tilde{q}}-q|\leq 1}\|\Delta_{\tilde{q}}BS_{\tilde{q}}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}.

We are going to deal with the term q~=q{\tilde{q}}=q only (the two other terms q~=q±1{\tilde{q}}=q\pm 1 can be estimated similarly). Applying successively Hölder’s inequality (in the variables tt and xx), Bernstein’s lemma, Young’s inequality (in the variable qq), and Hölder’s inequality (in the variable qq) gives

∑q2−q​‖Δq​B​Sq​E‖LT2​L2≤∑q2−q​‖Δq​B‖LT∞​L2​‖Sq​E‖LT2​L∞≤∑q2−q​∑j≤q‖Δq​B‖LT∞​L2​‖Δj​E‖LT2​L∞≤∑q∑j≤q2j−q​‖Δq​B‖LT∞​L2​‖Δj​E‖LT2​L2≤(∑q‖Δq​B‖LT∞​L22)1/2​(∑j‖Δj​E‖LT2​L22)1/2.\begin{split}\sum_{q}2^{-q}\|\Delta_{q}BS_{q}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}&\leq\sum_{q}2^{-q}\|\Delta_{q}B\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}}\|S_{q}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{\infty}}\\ &\leq\sum_{q}2^{-q}\sum_{j\leq q}\|\Delta_{q}B\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{\infty}}\\ &\leq\sum_{q}\sum_{j\leq q}2^{j-q}\|\Delta_{q}B\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\\ &\leq\left(\sum_{q}\|\Delta_{q}B\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{j}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}^{2}\right)^{1/2}.\end{split}

Next we prove (5.7). Applying Bernstein’s Lemma 3.1 and Cauchy-Schwarz (in jj) gives

‖S2​R​(B,E)‖L~T1​L2\displaystyle\|S_{2}R(B,E)\|_{\tilde{L}^{1}_{T}L^{2}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑q≤0‖Δq​R​(B,E)‖LT1​L2\displaystyle\sum_{q\leq 0}\|\Delta_{q}R(B,E)\|_{L^{1}_{T}L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑q≤02q​‖Δq​R​(B,E)‖LT1​L1\displaystyle\sum_{q\leq 0}2^{q}\|\Delta_{q}R(B,E)\|_{L^{1}_{T}L^{1}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑q≤02q​∑j≥q−2‖Δj​B‖LT2​L2​‖Δj​E‖LT2​L2\displaystyle\sum_{q\leq 0}2^{q}\sum_{j\geq q-2}\|\Delta_{j}B\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑j∑q≤inf(0,j+2)2q​‖Δj​B‖LT2​L2​‖Δj​E‖LT2​L2\displaystyle\sum_{j}\sum_{q\leq\inf(0,j+2)}2^{q}\|\Delta_{j}B\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑j≤02j​‖Δj​B‖LT2​L2​‖Δj​E‖LT2​L2+∑j≥0‖Δj​B‖LT2​L2​‖Δj​E‖LT2​L2\displaystyle\sum_{j\leq 0}2^{j}\|\Delta_{j}B\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}L^{2}}+\sum_{j\geq 0}\|\Delta_{j}B\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖E‖LT2​L2​‖B‖LT2​H˙1,0.\displaystyle\|E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\|B\|_{{L}^{2}_{T}\dot{H}^{1,0}}.

To estimate (5.8), Hölder’s inequality (in t,xt,x) and Cauchy-Schwarz (in jj) gives

‖(I−S2)​R​(E,B)‖L~T2​ℬ˙2,1−1\displaystyle\|(I-S_{2})R(E,B)\|_{{\tilde{L}}^{2}_{T}\dot{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}_{2,1}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑q≥0∑j≥q−2‖Δj​E‖LT2​L2​‖Δj​B‖LT∞​L2\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq 0}\sum_{j\geq q-2}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}B\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑j≥−2∑0≤q≤j+2‖Δj​E‖LT2​L2​‖Δj​B‖LT∞​L2\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq-2}\sum_{0\leq q\leq j+2}\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}B\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑j≥−2max⁡(j,1)​‖Δj​E‖LT2​L2​‖Δj​B‖LT∞​L2\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq-2}\max(j,1)\|\Delta_{j}E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}B\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖E‖LT2​Llog2​‖B‖LT∞​Llog2.\displaystyle\|E\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}_{\rm log}}\|B\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}_{\rm log}}.

Proof of (3.7) As for the proof of (3.6), we split u​BuB following the paraproduct decomposition:

u​B=TB​u+Tu​B+R⁡(u,B).uB=T_{B}u+T_{u}B+R(u,B).

We shall only estimate here TB​uT_{B}u, the estimate of R⁡(u,B)R(u,B) being similar, and that of Tu​BT_{u}B easier. By Hölder’s inequality,

‖TB​u‖LT2​Llog22=∑qmax⁡(1,q)​‖Sq​B​Δq​u‖LT2​L22≲∑qmax⁡(1,q)​‖Δq​u‖LT2​L22​‖Sq​B‖LT∞​L∞2.\begin{split}\left\|T_{B}u\right\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}_{\rm log}}^{2}&=\sum_{q}\max(1,q)\left\|S_{q}B\Delta_{q}u\right\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}^{2}\\ &\lesssim\sum_{q}\max(1,q)\left\|\Delta_{q}u\right\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}^{2}\left\|S_{q}B\right\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{\infty}}^{2}.\end{split}

Now observe that Bernstein’s lemma and Cauchy-Schwarz’ inequality (in jj) give

‖Sq​B‖LT∞​L∞≲∑j<q2j​‖Δj​B‖Lt∞​L2≲(∑j<q22​jmax⁡(1,q))1/2​‖B‖L~∞​Llog2≲2qmax⁡(1,q).\begin{split}\left\|S_{q}B\right\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{\infty}}&\lesssim\sum_{j<q}2^{j}\left\|\Delta_{j}B\right\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{2}}\\ &\lesssim\left(\sum_{j<q}\frac{2^{2j}}{\max(1,q)}\right)^{1/2}\|B\|_{\tilde{L}^{\infty}L^{2}_{\rm log}}\\ &\lesssim\frac{2^{q}}{\sqrt{\max(1,q)}}.\end{split}

‖TB​u‖LT2​Llog22≲∑22​q​‖Δq​u‖LT2​L22​‖B‖L~T∞​Llog22.\begin{split}\left\|T_{B}u\right\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}_{\rm log}}^{2}\lesssim\sum 2^{2q}\|\Delta_{q}u\|_{L^{2}_{T}L^{2}}^{2}\|B\|_{\tilde{L}^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}_{\rm log}}^{2}.\end{split}

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
